**Evaluate** when #132 is done.

## Why

When this is done, the agent's behavior can be checked again after any change to its instructions, its tools, or its model, by running a set of evaluations. Without them, the only way to tell whether a change made the agent better or worse is Joe testing by hand.

## Design

- [DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md), section 5.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 3.1 (tests).
- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 11.

## Open questions

- Which framework runs the evaluations? promptfoo is the likely choice. Check its current docs, and that it can run the app's coordinator through the Agent SDK on the Claude Max plan (systems design, section 5).
- How is each result scored: by what was saved, such as the trip brief and memory, by a model reading the reply, or both?
- How much of the Claude Max plan does one run of the evaluations use?
- How do the simulated user (#66) and the acceptance tests (#69) fit with the evaluations?
- ~~Do #66, #67, #68, and #69 still make sense as written? They're the testing and checking work after the workers, and they were planned before the evaluations in Phoenix and the evaluation issues, such as #167, #177, and #185. Look at them again together with this issue and those. Raised by Joe on 2026-10-28.~~ Settled 2026-11-04 in chat: #66 becomes the setup for a simulated user on any harness and model, such as Codex with a GPT model. It chats through `npm run live-chat` (#251), a terminal client for the app's API, signed in as its own Supabase user, and is shaken out with a whole San Francisco trip on the local stack. #67 and #68 become the first trips recorded on the live site for the corpus. They check how the simulated user behaved and what was saved to the trip brief, not that the itinerary matches domain model section 5, since live places and the workers' picks change from run to run. #69 stays as written. Traces in the `road-trip-agent-local` Phoenix project are throwaway, and the `road-trip-agent` project holds the sessions to evaluate.
- Which evaluations watch for these `update_trip_brief` mistakes? Tool descriptions start lean, with no example of a whole call. One is added only when an evaluation shows a mistake it would fix. The mistakes:
  - Sending every item on every call, when only one changed.
  - Splitting one change into a call per item.
  - Summarizing the user in a text item, such as `mustSeesText`, instead of using their words.
- Should an evaluation cover how an agent judges a place's budget tier, value, mid-range, or posh, at the edges between tiers? A place could fit two tiers, depending on how it's looked at. Nothing defines where one tier ends and the next starts yet (#60). Raised while going through the coordinator's view file, `src/agent/coordinator.view.md`.
- ~~Should an evaluation check that the coordinator keeps itinerary facts out of trip memory? No fact is kept in both (functional spec 5.2). In Joe's terminal run on 2026-10-23, the coordinator saved "Trip starts and ends in Austin. The user flies out of Austin the night of Sunday, February 14, 2027" to trip memory. The start and end places and the dates belong in the itinerary. The flight that evening belongs in memory, since the itinerary can't hold it. #55 changes the coordinator's memory instructions to say so. It also adds `update_itinerary`, so the evaluation can't run before #55 is merged. Raised by Joe on 2026-10-23, while settling #55's open questions.~~ Moved to #209 on 2026-10-28.
- May the coordinator add a note for itself to a memory item, beyond the user's words? In all five runs of the #132 spike, it did. "We never eat at chains" became "Never eats at chain restaurants. Suggest only independent, local places for meals." "Skip I-35 this time" became "Avoid I-35 on this trip. Plan routes out of Austin that don't use it, and set waypoints if a leg would default onto it." The judge's rubric didn't say whether that counts as a rule the user didn't state, so it graded the same wording both ways ([research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), section 2.5). Raised by the #132 spike on 2026-10-24.
- Should functional spec 10.2's example change? It gives "no chain restaurants" as trip memory, but the #48 check expects "we never eat at chains" in user memory. The "never" is what makes it a standing preference. Raised by the #132 spike on 2026-10-24.
- ~~How do the user's message and the right token counts get into each turn's trace? The Agent SDK instrumentation shows the streamed prompt as `{}`, and leaves cache tokens out of its input count, so a 48,255-token turn shows as 8. The spike branch fixes both with spans from our own code in place of the instrumentation: one for the turn, and one for each model call and each tool call, with each call's thinking and tokens. Workers aren't covered yet ([research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), sections 2.2 and 3). Raised by the #132 spike on 2026-10-24.~~ Moved to #135 on 2026-10-25.
- ~~How is `@arizeai/phoenix-client` installed for good? It names `@anthropic-ai/sdk` `^0.35.0` as an optional peer, and the app has 0.135.0, so `npm install` fails without `--legacy-peer-deps`. The spike tested an `overrides` entry in `package.json` that fixes it with no flag ([research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), section 3). Raised by the #132 spike on 2026-10-24.~~ Moved to #282 on 2026-11-05.
- Where do experiments send their traces and results? The #132 spike ran Phoenix on Joe's machine, under the `evals` Compose profile. #135 runs one Phoenix on the server, reached from Joe's machine through an SSH tunnel, with the server's traces in the `road-trip-agent` project and local ones in `road-trip-agent-local`. So the experiments could use that Phoenix too, through the tunnel, or a local Phoenix of their own. Raised on 2026-10-25, while writing #135.
- Which evaluations check how the coordinator finds a place the user names? #152 adds `find_in_trip`, which searches the trip's own places, next to `find_place`, which searches Google. So there are two tools for a place the user names. The coordinator should call `find_in_trip` first, and `find_place` only for a place that isn't in the trip (technical spec 5.2). `find_in_trip` always returns the 5 closest places, so the coordinator also has to notice when none is the place meant. Example: the user wants a new restaurant, Desert Rose Grill, and the closest match is the Desert Pearl Inn. It should ask, not select the inn. And when `select_user_place` says the place is also a candidate on another stop (#56), it should notice, and fix the pick or ask. Raised on 2026-10-26, from #129 ([research/itinerary-read-size.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/itinerary-read-size.md), sections 6.3 and 6.4).
- Should the agents' prompts go in Phoenix's prompt registry? It keeps versions of a prompt, and its playground and experiments can run one against saved spans. It doesn't link a prompt to traces by itself: the app would set `llm.prompt_template.version` on the spans. #194 puts the app's commit SHA on each turn's span, and the view files at that commit show each agent's prompt and tools, so a registry version isn't needed just to see what an agent read. Our prompts are built in code, so the registry would hold a second copy. Raised on 2026-10-28, while settling #194. The judge prompts fit better. A rubric is one model call with a few slots, which is what Phoenix's playground runs. So rubric versions could be tried there against the judge's dataset, turns labeled by Joe, and compared turn by turn. Raised on 2026-11-03, in chat.
- Should a walkthrough of the prompts decide which behaviors get an evaluation? The design walkthroughs (reviews/walkthroughs/) had a fresh agent read only the design docs and play the user and every agent through the San Francisco and Moab trips, and they found many design gaps before any code existed. The same could be done with the agents' instructions and tool descriptions, as the view files show them: give an agent a view file and a trip, and have it say what it would call, and why. A problem that's clearly a wording mistake gets fixed, since a clear fix goes in without an evaluation. One where it's unclear whether a change helps becomes an evaluation candidate. Running it with a smaller model, such as Sonnet, may show where the wording leans on Opus to fill gaps. Caveat: a model saying what it would do isn't the same as what it does deep in a real conversation, so this finds wording problems, not behavior. Running the real coordinator with faked tool replies and a model playing the user would show behavior.
- When should real traces be scored after the fact? Phoenix can run evaluators over traces that already exist, and attach the scores to their spans, with nothing run again. Code would pick out the suspect cases, and a judge model would decide the fuzzy ones. Example: code finds each `find_place` call with no earlier `find_in_trip` call in the session. A judge then decides whether the place was one the user named, and whether an earlier search was for the same place, such as "Desert Rose" and "Desert Rose Grill". Some mistakes need only code, such as an `update_trip_brief` call that resends an item with the value it already had. A score over traces is a rate, such as 3 of 40 turns, not a pass or fail. There are few real traces today, so this waits until simulations or walkthroughs make more. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-03, in chat.
- How are the evaluations built up? This is a provisional plan, not a commitment. It's what we're working toward, and it can change as we go. Sketched by Joe and Claude in chat on 2026-11-03, after running Phoenix's built-in evaluators on the Bar Harbor session:
  - Joe learns more of Phoenix first, through its tutorials.
  - Record more sessions to build a corpus. Joe and his wife each plan a trip. Simulated users play the San Francisco and Moab trips on the live site (#66, #67, #68). Any harness and model can play one, such as Claude Code, a GPT model through Codex, or an open-weight model.
  - A simulated user gets a trip file, a persona file, and its instructions, with no hooks steering it (#66). The trip file holds the facts it knows (dates, places, budget, driving limits), things it hasn't decided, and changes partway through, such as skipping Denver once the first draft is done. The persona file says how it talks, such as curt or impatient. Its prompt says to answer only what's asked, give one or two facts at a time, and stick with any answer it makes up. The trip file also works as an answer key, to check what the agent saved to the trip brief.
  - Write one general evaluator first, to learn the process. It covers how the agent does on any turn, not one behavior. Phoenix's built-in rubrics don't fit a long planning conversation: on Bar Harbor, correctness marked 22 of 23 turns incorrect. So the rubric is our own, using the built-ins only as a starting point. Start with "grounded in the record": every place, hour, distance, or price in a reply comes from a tool result or the trip record. Two strong models, such as Opus and a GPT 6.1 model, label turns from the corpus, each on its own. Code compares their labels, and Joe looks only at the turns where they disagree. No turns are labeled by hand. Then compare the judge's labels to theirs, and refine the rubric until they agree. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat. The corpus is the sessions with a `corpus` session annotation in the `road-trip-agent` Phoenix project: 21 sessions, 3 `real_user` and 18 `simulated_user`, labeled on 2026-11-05. The first general evaluator, "grounded in the record", moved to #282 on 2026-11-05, with what it checks, what the judge reads, and how the labeling runs. Two or three general evaluators may follow, such as these:
    - "Request handled": the reply does what the user asked.
    - "The reply is for the user": it tells the user what they need to know, and doesn't think out loud. On a new trip, one reply began "I need to read brief and memory first." That's a note the coordinator wrote to itself, before its tool calls, and the user saw it. #65 adds a line to the instructions against it. This evaluator shows whether it still happens. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-04, in chat.
    - "Fits the trip": what the reply says makes sense given the itinerary. In #282's sample, a Moab reply chose a hotel and said "after a day of hiking, you'll also have a pool and a hot breakfast there". Its Day 2 leaves the hotel at 5:30 a.m. and doesn't come back until 8:02 p.m., so the hot breakfast doesn't fit that day. Each fact had a source, so "grounded in the record" passes it. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, while reviewing #282's first set.
    - "Tool use": it picks the right tool, with the right inputs, and doesn't call tools it doesn't need. Phoenix's built-in evaluators for tool use didn't work well on Bar Harbor, so the rubric is our own. It also answers a question moved from #65 on 2026-11-04: are about two dozen tools too many for the coordinator? If it chooses badly, merge the add, update, and remove tools for each kind of item.
  - The judge sees what the agent saw: the coordinator's system prompt from the commit on the turn's span, and the earlier turns with their tool calls. On Bar Harbor, adding that context changed tool response handling from 21 of 23 turns incorrect to 10.
  - Then write the behavior evaluations: the issues labeled "Eval Canidate", plus the ones listed in this issue. They can start from recorded sessions with `npm run run-turn` (#245), before any simulation exists.
  - Then run more simulated sessions (#66) to grow the corpus. Run both kinds of evaluation on them. A general evaluator gives a rate over many turns, such as 3 of 40. A behavior evaluation passes or fails on a case built to trigger the behavior.
- Do the evaluations run as Phoenix experiments, written in TypeScript? A dataset row would name a recorded turn (session, turn, and message) and what's expected of it. The experiment's task runs that turn with `npm run run-turn`, and code checks and judges score the result. Phoenix keeps each experiment's results, so a run before a prompt change and a run after it can be compared case by case. Joe leans toward TypeScript for the real evaluations, since they'd reuse app code such as `run-turn`, even though his Phoenix tutorials are in Python. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-03, in chat.

## Do

- Set up the framework, and a command that runs the evaluations against the local stack (systems design, section 6), outside `npm run check`.
- Start an evaluation of one turn from a recorded session with `npm run run-turn` (#245). It gives the coordinator the recorded conversation and the trip as it stood, and runs the turn on today's code. Leave the copied transcript lines as they are. The API drops each of the coordinator's earlier thinking blocks once anything before it in the conversation changes. In #245, rewriting the first message's date line dropped all 17 of them in the Bar Harbor session's turn 5 (persistence design, section 8.9).
- Watch the runs for the coordinator reacting to the two lines Claude Code adds that the recorded turn didn't have: its date change line, and an environment line with the local working folder (persistence design, section 8.9). #245 accepted both. If the coordinator reacts to either, look at it again.
- Turn the checks in #48 into evaluations: discovery fills in the trip brief, user or trip memory, confirming the usual driving hours on a second trip, and pushing back on 14 hours of driving.
- Write how the evaluations run into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5, in place of "How they run is settled when the first one is written."

## Done when

- One command runs every evaluation and prints each result.
- Each evaluation passes against the current coordinator. A change made on purpose to break one, such as taking the driving hours line out of the instructions, makes it fail.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.

---

Moved from the [development plan](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/plan/development-plan.md#phase-14a-agent-evaluations).
